editions.title: Nvidia's Huang scandal wipes $190bn as AI sell-off lingers
editions.notification: Nvidia loses $190bn in a day as CEO Jensen Huang faces an investigation over a China-linked affair.
editions.intro:
The dominant story is the scandal engulfing Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang. He has acknowledged an affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, whom US officials reportedly concluded passed information to Chinese government channels. Nvidia's board has launched an independent investigation, Congress has asked for a briefing by 11 November, and a class action alleges shareholders were misled. Nvidia shares closed down 4.3% on Monday, wiping roughly $190bn from its market value. Reports also suggest Moonshot AI accessed top Nvidia chips in China despite export curbs, which, if confirmed, would sharpen the debate over export controls.

Elsewhere, the AI sector is moving fast. Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, with company-reported gains in speed and coding and lower prices, and reports say it is preparing a large IPO, with a valuation of up to $1.4tn. Google's Gemini 4 Carbon became generally available, and Meta launched a small, cheap model. Asian markets rebounded after a steep AI-led rout, while AMD forecast record revenue and said it expects to outsell Intel for the first time in a quarter.

Regulation and security also featured. Washington is weighing a ban on Chinese optical transceivers, which Microsoft is lobbying against, and the UK may widen its under-16 social media ban to marketplaces such as Vinted and eBay. Binance was reported to have lost $6.3bn in what Bloomberg calls the largest crypto heist on record.

top_stories.title: Huang admits affair; Nvidia board opens investigation
top_stories.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang acknowledged an affair with Alice Huang, whom US officials reportedly linked to Chinese intelligence. Nvidia's board has opened an independent investigation, and House Republicans want a briefing by 11 November. The Chinese embassy denies the allegations.

top_stories.summary: A federal class action in California accuses Nvidia and Huang of misleading shareholders. Nvidia shares closed down 4.3% on Monday, wiping roughly $190bn off the market value. Donald Trump said the FBI was looking into the matter.

top_stories.title: Anthropic launches Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2
top_stories.summary: Anthropic says both models are faster and better at coding and research, with prices cut to $8 and $40 per million input and output tokens. Mythos is limited to vetted users. The benchmark figures are company-reported.

top_stories.title: Anthropic reportedly targets IPO valuation of up to $1.4tn
top_stories.summary: The Financial Times reports Anthropic plans a listing valuing it at up to $1.4tn and raising as much as $64bn. Bloomberg adds that a live-streamed event with Dario Amodei and Jamie Dimon is being planned. Neither has been officially confirmed.

top_stories.title: Asian stocks rebound after AI-led rout
top_stories.summary: Asian markets rallied after a steep sell-off driven by AI-related shares had pushed several regional indices into bear market territory. The feed gives few figures, so the size of the recovery is unclear.

top_stories.title: AMD forecasts record revenue and may outsell Intel
top_stories.summary: AMD guided fourth-quarter revenue to about $17bn after a 45% rise in the third quarter. Data centre sales nearly doubled on Instinct accelerators. If forecasts hold, AMD would outsell Intel in a single quarter for the first time.

top_stories.title: Microsoft lobbies against US ban on Chinese optical gear
top_stories.summary: The FCC is considering an import ban on Chinese optical transceivers, which supply about two-thirds of the global market. Microsoft and the IT Industry Council are lobbying against it, arguing a ban could sharply cut supply for US data centres.

editions.title: Huang affair scandal rattles Nvidia as Anthropic readies IPO
editions.notification: Nvidia's Jensen Huang admits an affair as a probe into alleged Chinese spying begins. Shares slip.
editions.intro:
The biggest story is the scandal engulfing Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang. He has publicly apologised for an affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom US intelligence reportedly believes was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security. Nvidia's board has launched an independent investigation and says it has no reason to believe sensitive information or national security was compromised. Nvidia shares fell more than 4% on Monday, while broader US indices rose. Analysts say the affair could sharpen scrutiny of chip exports to China, and Congressional chairs have asked for a briefing by 11 November. The suspected operation has not been independently confirmed, and the Chinese government and embassy deny the espionage claims.

The scandal sits alongside reports that point to the same underlying question: how China accesses advanced AI chips. Bloomberg reports that Moonshot AI used a large pool of Nvidia's top chips this summer, despite US export restrictions, and Wired reports Huang hired a crisis PR firm a year before he acknowledged the affair. Meanwhile AMD said it expects to outsell Intel for the first time in a single quarter, on AI accelerator demand.

In AI model news, Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, with prices cut to $8 and $40 per million input and output tokens. Bloomberg also reports Anthropic is planning a live-streamed IPO discussion between Dario Amodei and Jamie Dimon, though this is unconfirmed. Asian markets rebounded after a sharp AI-led sell-off, and Australia announced mandatory AI incident reporting after an OpenAI agent breach.

editions.title: Nvidia's Jensen Huang faces board probe over spy reports
editions.notification: Nvidia's CEO is under an independent probe over reported China spy links. Here's what we know so far.
editions.intro:
The dominant story is the crisis at Nvidia. Chief executive Jensen Huang has apologised in an internal memo for an affair, after The New York Times reported that US agencies were examining Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive, over suspected links to China's Ministry of State Security. Nvidia's board has opened an independent investigation, supported by outside counsel, and says it sees no sign that national security or company secrets were compromised. Huang remains CEO. Three Republican House committee chairs have asked for a briefing by 11 November, and Singapore has opened its own probe into Megaspeed. The Chinese government and embassy deny the espionage allegations, and no one has been charged. The suspected operation has not been independently confirmed.

The episode matters well beyond gossip. Nvidia sits at the centre of AI chip supply, and Megaspeed reportedly bought billions of dollars of its chips, while the US Commerce Department has accused the firm of smuggling $2 billion of advanced chips to China. Nvidia shares fell more than 9% in a single session, their steepest daily drop since January 2025, amid a wider chip sell-off that also hit Asian markets. Analysts such as Jeffrey Sonnenfeld put Huang's chances of surviving the probe at roughly even.

Elsewhere, the AI-infrastructure backlash is gathering pace. A new analysis found about 90% of public comments at local government meetings opposed data centres, a Michigan Democrat who campaigned against them won a seat in Congress, and a Texas town-level ban passed with about 77% support. Samsung and SK hynix together hold 329 trillion won in cash, funding record chip spending and shareholder returns.

top_stories.title: Huang apologises for affair as board opens independent probe
top_stories.summary: Nvidia's CEO admitted an affair in a letter to staff, while the board said it has no reason to believe secrets or national security were compromised. An independent committee will investigate reported intelligence concerns over Alice Huang, whom US officials reportedly linked to Beijing. The suspected operation has not been independently confirmed.

top_stories.title: House chairs call Huang to closed-door briefing
top_stories.summary: Three Republican House committee chairs have arranged a closed-door meeting with Huang over national security concerns tied to Megaspeed. Singapore has opened its own probe, and Nvidia says its customer meetings are routine. The briefing is due by 11 November.

top_stories.title: Analysts weigh whether Huang can survive the probe
top_stories.summary: Yale's Jeffrey Sonnenfeld puts Huang's odds of staying on at about 50-50. The affair raises questions about Nvidia's AI investments and its dealings with Megaspeed, which bought about $2 billion of chips. Investors will watch the investigation's findings closely.

The deal is unconfirmed and Brightspeed is reportedly close to bankruptcy. The report followed a steep one-day fall in Nvidia shares.

SK hynix is ramping HBM4 output with 14 long-term supply deals. Investors now want cash returns, not just growth.

editions.title: Tech sell-off deepens as Anthropic presses on with IPO and Nvidia faces spy claims
editions.notification: Tech shares slump after the midterms, Tesla winds down Cybertruck, and Anthropic eyes a pre-Thanksgiving IPO.
editions.intro:
Tech markets were rattled this week. The Nasdaq 100 fell 6.4 percent on Thursday, partly recovering on Friday, as rising borrowing costs, heavy AI spending and Democratic midterm wins raised fears of slower data-centre construction. Tesla shares fell 11 percent after Elon Musk said Cybertruck production will wind down around mid-2027, with the Texas plant shifting to the Cybercab robotaxi and Optimus robots. SpaceX dropped 9 percent in the same session, and Musk's fortune reportedly fell by $113bn.

Against that backdrop, Anthropic is reportedly pressing ahead with an IPO before Thanksgiving, seeking $80 to $100 billion at a valuation of $1.25 to $1.75 trillion, below some investors' hopes. OpenAI has reportedly trimmed its funding-round target and raised only about a third of what it sought, though a separate report claims $11bn new funding at a $1.25 trillion valuation. Both are unconfirmed in the material provided.

Nvidia faces its own storm. Three House committee chairs have arranged a closed-door meeting with Jensen Huang over reports that Megaspeed executive Alice Huang may have been recruited by China's intelligence services. Nvidia says its customer contacts are routine, and China has dismissed the claims. Meanwhile, the memory boom continues: DRAM prices are soaring, Samsung's cash pile passed 200 trillion won, and Raspberry Pi and Oppo are feeling the squeeze. Samsung's Taylor, Texas plant may start trial runs in December.

top_stories.title: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck as Musk pivots to robotaxis and robots
top_stories.summary: Musk said on X that Cybertruck production at Texas will end around mid-2027, freeing space for Cybercab and Optimus. Tesla shares fell 11 percent on Thursday, with SpaceX down 9 percent, after Musk-backed Republicans lost the midterms.

top_stories.title: Anthropic reportedly pushes ahead with IPO at a lower valuation
top_stories.summary: The FT reports Anthropic wants to raise $80 to $100 billion before Thanksgiving at $1.25 to $1.75 trillion, below the $2 trillion some hoped for. The move comes amid a broad tech sell-off, and OpenAI has reportedly trimmed its own funding target.

top_stories.title: Congress calls Jensen Huang over reported Chinese spy link
top_stories.summary: House chairs have asked Nvidia's chief to explain links to Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who was reportedly watched by US agencies over China ties. Neither has been charged, and Nvidia says it would be warned if the government saw a threat.

top_stories.title: Samsung's Texas foundry may begin trial runs in December
top_stories.summary: Samsung's Taylor plant could start trial operations in mid-to-late December, with mass production next year. The site is expected to make Tesla's AI6 chips under a $16.5 billion deal, though the project is about two years late.

top_stories.title: No end in sight for the GPU and memory squeeze
top_stories.summary: DRAM prices are reportedly up about 400 percent since 2024, and Nvidia's RTX 5090 sells well above its launch price. Major memory makers are shifting capacity to AI memory and expect tight supply through 2027 and 2028.

top_stories.title: Samsung's cash pile passes 200 trillion won
top_stories.summary: Samsung reported 214.8 trillion won in cash at the end of Q3 and plans record capital spending of 84.4 trillion won. It can return 90 to 110 trillion won to shareholders this year.

top_stories.title: METR says Anthropic may have crossed its AI acceleration warning line
top_stories.summary: METR's audit suggests Anthropic's rate of model improvement has roughly doubled, with much of the speed-up attributed to AI helping its own research. METR still rates acute catastrophic risk as low, but says the public risk report understated the acceleration.

editions.title: Tech sell-off deepens as Anthropic eyes $1.5tn IPO
editions.notification: AI stocks slump, Anthropic reportedly eyes a $1.5tn IPO, and Tesla winds down the Cybertruck. Here's the morning brief.
editions.intro:
A sharp tech-led sell-off dominated the period, with the Nasdaq Composite falling 5.5% at one point before recovering 1.1% on Friday. Investors pointed to doubts about returns on AI spending and to the US midterm results, where Democrats' gains raised fears of slower AI development. Asian markets were hit hard, with South Korea's Kospi down 6% and SK Hynix dropping more than 10%, while the FTSE 100 slipped after the Bank of England raised rates.

Against that backdrop, the AI giants are still pressing ahead. The Financial Times reports that Anthropic intends to go ahead with an IPO targeting a valuation of about $1.5tn, with a listing before Thanksgiving. Bloomberg reports OpenAI has been valued at $1.25tn in a fresh round, below the $1.4tn it had hoped for. Political pressure is rising too: Senator Bernie Sanders and several newly elected Democrats are calling for datacentre pauses, and Microsoft is reportedly winding down an Oracle AI-compute rental, a blow to Oracle's shares.

Elsewhere, Tesla confirmed it will end Cybertruck production in Texas around 2027 to make room for Cybercab and Optimus, though Tesla shares rose on Friday after falling 11% the day before. Nvidia reportedly told foreign cloud customers to generate at least half their revenue outside China, a sign of tightening US export pressure. Samsung's mobile staff are protesting over pay as the phone division heads for its first annual loss.

top_stories.title: Anthropic reportedly presses ahead with $1.5tn IPO
top_stories.summary: The Financial Times reports Anthropic plans to go ahead with its IPO despite the sell-off, targeting about $1.5tn and a listing before Thanksgiving. The timing and terms may still change, but a listing would be one of the largest in tech history.

top_stories.title: AI stocks rebound after trillions wiped from markets
top_stories.summary: A tech-led sell-off spread from the US to Asia and Europe, with the Nasdaq partly recovering on Friday. Strong US jobs data and doubts about AI returns and midterm politics drove the volatility.

top_stories.title: OpenAI valued at $1.25tn in smaller-than-hoped round
top_stories.summary: OpenAI's new round values it at $1.25tn, below the $1.4tn it had sought, as tech stocks fell and public opposition to AI grew. Altman says OpenAI will wait for stronger safety claims before listing.

top_stories.title: Democrats push for datacentre pauses after midterms
top_stories.summary: Sanders and newly elected Democrats are calling for national or state pauses on datacentre construction, and voters passed local restrictions. The White House says existing projects will largely continue, but investors are nervous.

top_stories.title: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production
top_stories.summary: Musk said Cybertruck output in Texas will end around 2027 to free capacity for Cybercab and Optimus. Cybertruck sales fell to about 20,000 in 2025, far below earlier forecasts, and Tesla's shares were volatile.

top_stories.title: Nvidia reportedly requires foreign clouds to earn most revenue outside China
top_stories.summary: The FT reports Nvidia now requires foreign cloud providers to make at least 51% of revenue from outside China, applied to future deals. It follows tighter US export scrutiny and could hit Asian cloud operators.

top_stories.summary: Bloomberg reports Microsoft will not renew a 2023 deal to rent AI capacity from Oracle, and is reassessing over $80bn of other cloud contracts. Oracle shares fell about 3% and the company is under credit pressure.

editions.title: Tech shares slump as US midterms revive AI slowdown fears
editions.notification: Nasdaq's worst day in 18 months as Democrats' midterm win sparks data centre curbs fears. Here's what's next.
editions.intro:
Global tech shares suffered their sharpest sell-off in well over a year after Democrats won both houses of Congress in the midterm elections. Investors expect tighter scrutiny of AI data centres, with Democrats having promised a national moratorium on new facilities. The Nasdaq Composite fell about 5.5 per cent on Thursday, its worst day in 18 months, and entered correction territory, wiping out an estimated $2tn to $2.5tn. Nvidia fell 9.2 per cent, and chipmakers including AMD, Micron and Infineon were hit hard across markets.

The contagion spread quickly. Japan's Nikkei dropped below 60,000 points for the first time since May, falling 6.3 per cent at one point, while South Korea's Kospi triggered a circuit breaker after falling more than 8 per cent. Taiwan had its worst week since 2001. The sell-off has also reached credit markets, with SoftBank leading losses in Asian dollar bonds, and Indian equities were among the few gainers in the region. The FTSE 100 was little changed, closing down 0.4 per cent.

The political backdrop is now central to the industry's outlook. Elon Musk spent around $450m backing Republicans and still saw losses, including in Texas, and his companies Tesla and SpaceX fell. OpenAI and Amazon have responded with pledges to drop NDAs with officials and to cover power costs for data centre projects. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has blamed opponents for the fall, so the policy direction for AI infrastructure will be a key thing to watch.

top_stories.title: Global tech stocks plunge as midterms revive AI slowdown fears
top_stories.summary: Tech shares fell across the US, Europe and Asia after Democrats took both houses of Congress, with campaigns focused on slowing data centre growth. Around $2.5tn was wiped from the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 fell 4.4 per cent. Democrats have promised a national data centre moratorium, which investors are pricing in.

top_stories.title: Nasdaq suffers worst day in 18 months, enters correction
top_stories.summary: The Nasdaq Composite fell about 5.5 per cent on Thursday, with Nvidia down 9.2 per cent and the VIX up 61 per cent. Investors are betting that new Democratic governors and lawmakers will curb datacentre expansion. The FTSE 100 closed down 0.4 per cent.

top_stories.title: Asian tech shares sink as Nikkei and Kospi slide
top_stories.summary: The Nikkei 225 dropped below 60,000 for the first time since May, and the Kospi fell under 5,000. The falls followed fears of tighter US regulation of AI data centres after the midterms.

top_stories.title: Musk's midterm spending fails to deliver Republican wins
top_stories.summary: Elon Musk spent almost $450m backing Republicans, more than anyone in a single cycle, but Democrat James Talarico beat Republican Ken Paxton in Texas. The result could bring tougher scrutiny of SpaceX and tech firms, and Tesla and SpaceX shares fell.

top_stories.title: OpenAI pulls back from NDAs for data centre projects
top_stories.summary: OpenAI pledged to drop NDAs with public officials, pay the full cost of its electricity and infrastructure, and publish local job forecasts. The move follows voter opposition to data centre expansion and mirrors an Amazon pledge.

Finance.title: Nvidia shaken by CEO affair probe as US inflation runs hot
Finance.notification: Nvidia shares slide again as the Huang affair probe deepens, with Microsoft now the bigger company
Finance.summary:
The biggest story is the fall in Nvidia shares after chief executive Jensen Huang admitted an affair with a woman US intelligence reportedly believes is a Chinese spy. The stock has lost more than 11% since Monday, a board-led investigation is under way, a class action has been filed, and Microsoft has overtaken Nvidia on market value. Analysts warn of further falls if Huang steps down.

Alongside this, hotter-than-expected US consumer prices for October have pushed traders to price in a Federal Reserve rate rise in December. Treasuries sold off, the dollar firmed, gold fell and Wall Street's rebound from last week's AI-related sell-off was tested. Anthropic is pressing ahead with an IPO targeting a valuation of up to $1.4tn, a move that will test investor appetite for AI.

In the UK, the FTSE 100 closed slightly lower after early gains faded, while Marks & Spencer rose after its capital markets day. Vodafone posted a large half-year loss from a German impairment but lifted its full-year guidance. Europe and Asia are seeing a split: Asian chip stocks rallied on strong AI demand and China's record trade surplus, while Seoul's Kospi endured a steep sell-off and emergency margin-loan relief.

World.title: US midterm fallout, Iran de-escalation and hot inflation weigh on markets
World.notification: Hot inflation data, Trump's Iran signals and a Democratic House reshape the week's markets
World.summary:
The biggest story in world affairs today is the fallout from the US midterm elections, where Democrats have won the House and are expected to take the Senate. Trump has blamed the result on a 'giant step back' and a one-day stock loss of about $3 trillion, while Republicans are split over the Iran war and the push by Congressman Thomas Massie to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth. Markets are also reacting to an October inflation report that came in hotter than expected and has raised talk of a Federal Reserve rate rise in December.

Trump says Iran is militarily 'effectively over' and that renewed strikes are unlikely, a message that helped push oil lower. Iranian officials remain doubtful, and European ministers at the G7 in Paris say they cannot rule out fresh escalation over the Strait of Hormuz. Abu Dhabi hosts the first trilateral Russia-Ukraine-US talks since February, with European leaders pressing to be included.

For investors, the picture is mixed: softer oil on diplomacy, a possible rate rise from inflation, and a new Congress that could bring tougher oversight of large companies, including Nvidia and tech firms.

Tech.title: Nvidia chief Huang faces affair probe as AI shares wobble
Tech.notification: Nvidia's Jensen Huang admits an affair with an executive US officials reportedly linked to China. Shares slid.
Tech.summary:
The dominant tech story is the fallout around Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang. He has acknowledged in an internal memo an affair with Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore-based data centre company, after reports that US officials believed she had shared information with Beijing. Nvidia says no sensitive information was shared, its board has opened an independent investigation, and House Republican chairs want a briefing by 11 November. Nvidia shares fell more than 4% on Monday, and a class action has been filed in California.

The affair story sits against a wider sell-off in AI-related shares, which has pushed several Asian markets into bear territory, with Asian indices now rebounding. The same week brought a wave of AI and chip news: Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, reports suggest it is preparing an IPO at up to $1.4 trillion, and AMD said it expects to outsell Intel for the first time. Policy pressure is also rising, with Washington weighing tighter controls on advanced chip flows to China and the FCC considering a ban on Chinese optical transceivers.

Beyond chips, the UK is weighing whether its under-16 social media ban should reach marketplaces such as Vinted and eBay, and Apple faces scrutiny over subscription sign-ups in its US stores.

highlights.label: Nvidia probe
highlights.text: Nvidia's board is investigating Huang, who says he supports the review. Analysts think the affair could speed up scrutiny of China chip exports.

highlights.label: Anthropic
highlights.text: Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 are out, with company-reported gains in coding and research and lower prices per million tokens.

highlights.label: AMD vs Intel
highlights.text: AMD forecasts Q4 revenue of about $17bn, which would top Intel's $15-16bn guidance if both hold, driven by AI accelerators.

highlights.label: Markets
highlights.text: Asian stocks rebounded after an AI-led rout that pushed many regional indices into bear market territory.

highlights.label: IPO wave
highlights.text: Reports say Anthropic is targeting a valuation of up to $1.4tn and could raise $64bn, though this is unconfirmed.

highlights.label: Gaming
highlights.text: Take-Two says GTA 6 presales are far above expectations ahead of the 19 November launch; Rockstar has not confirmed figures.

points.text: A US class action accuses Nvidia and Huang of misleading shareholders; Nvidia shares closed down 4.3%, wiping roughly $190bn.
Microsoft is reportedly lobbying against a possible FCC ban on Chinese optical transceivers, which make up about 66% of supply.
Bloomberg reports $6.3bn was stolen from Binance in what it calls the largest crypto heist on record; $3.13bn is still held by hackers.
Apple has reminded US Apple Store staff to get consent for subscription trials after videos alleged enrolments without clear agreement.
Alibaba's AI chip unit T-Head has filed for a Hong Kong IPO, the first formal step; size and valuation are not yet known.
Trump has nominated Palantir's security chief Michael LoSapio to lead CISA, ending a nearly two-year vacancy.

Fashion.title: Creative director hires lift resale and luxury buzz
Fashion.notification: New creative directors are reshaping luxury demand, and resale prices are following them
Fashion.summary:
The clearest thread in luxury today is the power of new creative directors. An eBay Watchlist report, published 10 November, shows searches for Matthieu Blazy rose 291% after his first Chanel collection, with Demna up 42% after his first Gucci show and Jonathan Anderson up 92% after his Dior debut. Resale is turning that attention into prices, with celebrity sightings also driving sales.

Creative change is reshaping the houses themselves. Martine Rose has been named creative director of Balenciaga, succeeding Pierpaolo Piccioli, a historic first for the house. Balenciaga is also marking the 25th anniversary of the Le City bag with a Damien Hirst capsule. Elsewhere, Vaccarello's final Saint Laurent show featured 49 gold looks, and Moncler's Remo Ruffini credits collaborations for keeping the brand relevant.

On the business side, On reported sales up 17.2% with Asia-Pacific growing 31.9%, while Safilo's nine-month adjusted EBITDA rose 32.7%. Brands are leaning on collaborations and new markets to keep momentum, even as The Children's Place, which owns Gymboree, has filed for Chapter 11 and is seeking a sale.

highlights.label: Balenciaga
highlights.text: Martine Rose takes over as creative director, succeeding Pierpaolo Piccioli. The appointment is a historic first for the Kering house.

highlights.label: Resale
highlights.text: eBay data shows new creative directors lifting secondhand demand, with Chanel's Matthieu Blazy searches up 291% after his first collection.

highlights.label: On
highlights.text: Sales rose 17.2% in the third quarter and Asia-Pacific grew 31.9%. The brand expects mid-to-high 20s growth in coming quarters.

highlights.label: Safilo
highlights.text: Q3 sales rose 3% with North America up 7.7%. Adjusted EBITDA rose 17.3% and CEO Angelo Trocchia's contract was renewed.

highlights.label: Children's Place
highlights.text: The Gymboree owner filed for Chapter 11 and plans an asset sale. Bids are due 9 December and stores remain open.

highlights.label: Moncler
highlights.text: Remo Ruffini says the brand now generates around €3bn in sales. Re/Icons, an archive-inspired collection, launches this autumn.

points.text: JLR accuses BYD of reverse-engineering a Defender rival; Dutch court bailiffs raided BYD offices in August.
Rick Owens's Adidas springblade line goes on sale 17 November, priced from $590 to $850.
Amex and Marriott Bonvoy add a no-annual-fee Canadian card from 9 February 2027.
Adidas Campus 00s Winter boot brings a laceless, UGG-style look, currently sold mainly in children's sizes.
Acer's October revenue rose 24.3%, its highest October figure in five years.
Shiseido returned to profit and raised full-year guidance, according to a brief headline report.

highlights.label: On
highlights.text: Sales rose 17.2% in the third quarter and Asia-Pacific grew 31.9%. The brand expects mid-to-high 20s growth in coming quarters.

highlights.label: Safilo
highlights.text: Q3 sales rose 3% with North America up 7.7%. Adjusted EBITDA rose 17.3% and CEO Angelo Trocchia's contract was renewed.

highlights.label: Children's Place
highlights.text: The Gymboree owner filed for Chapter 11 and plans an asset sale. Bids are due 9 December and stores remain open.

highlights.label: Moncler
highlights.text: Remo Ruffini says the brand now generates around €3bn in sales. Re/Icons, an archive-inspired collection, launches this autumn.

points.text: JLR accuses BYD of reverse-engineering a Defender rival; Dutch court bailiffs raided BYD offices in August.
Rick Owens's Adidas springblade line goes on sale 17 November, priced from $590 to $850.
Amex and Marriott Bonvoy add a no-annual-fee Canadian card from 9 February 2027.
Adidas Campus 00s Winter boot brings a laceless, UGG-style look, currently sold mainly in children's sizes.
Acer's October revenue rose 24.3%, its highest October figure in five years.
Shiseido returned to profit and raised full-year guidance, according to a brief headline report.
